key_idea: Consistency forces every guess to reuse the same y known characters on its yellow cells (never twice in the same column) and fresh characters on gray cells, so the yellow cells plus a secret row form a bipartite row/column graph that must be properly edge-coloured with y colours, which Konig's theorem guarantees once every column degree is at most y.
sketch: Let y be the number of Y per row. Necessary and sufficient: every column has at most y yellows, at least y columns have fewer than y yellows (the secret must place each known character in a column where it was never yellow), and Sigma >= y + (N+1)(M-y) because every gray cell and every non-known secret cell needs a brand new character. Add the secret as row N+1 with yellow cells on any y non-saturated columns, then edge-colour the bipartite graph with y colours using alternating-path (Kempe chain) flips, O(E*(N+M)) with E <= 1e4. Colour c becomes character c+1 and gray cells get increasing fresh numbers from y+1. Pitfalls: N is the number of rows and M the length (reversed from the prose), y=0 still needs (N+1)*M distinct characters. Multiple answers are accepted, so the sample checker shows a mismatch on sample 1; output was confirmed with my own validator (replays the game, checks colours against the secret and consistency of each guess with all earlier clues) and feasibility was compared with an exhaustive brute force on 400 tiny cases.
